doc.title: Ray Blue interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 23, 2022

title: Cross-Cultural Connection, Cape Town workshops and family
summary: Blue founded the nonprofit after teaching township students in Cape Town, started it in Cedar Rapids, and mentions his sons.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: This is your Cross-Cultural Connection, Inc. is that correct?
Was there a moment you remember that set you on this path?

You know when I was in graduate school I thought about how do I find grants for different things. And — because there’s different kinds of programming I was thinking about wanting to do and then it came to a point I was invited to play at the North Sea Jazz

Festival in Cape Town. And being there, while there the organizers asked me to be one of the clinicians, a clinician to do a workshop. Hotep Galeta, the pianist, the great South African pianist, he and I did a workshop for township students in Cape Town. And from that point it was amazing, he was amazing, the feeling of the teaching and the response and the passion of the students for the music and how, what the music felt like for us, you know how we shared it. And from that point then I was asked to do a few other workshops while I was there. And that’s how it started you know. So I’ll say my whole piece started in South Africa. And what I wanted to do was to be able to bring people together so they had an opportunity to learn about one another by communicating with one another, not depending on what was in the newspaper or in a news broadcast. If you want to know how this person who lives in a township in South Africa, how they feel about certain things, ask them. You’ll have an accurate answer. You know? So we brought people together through the music. And usually a part of my sessions is we would have dialogue with one another. You know? There were folks in the session who were also from South Africa who didn’t know each other. They didn’t know each other, but they began to talk to one another. And they found what they had in common or what they didn’t have in common. You know? But what you learned you have the ability now to understand from a clearer perspective. You know? Yeah.
We could use a good dose of that these days.

And you know this. Absolutely. Yeah. But that’s how it started. But then so whenever I would go, whenever I’d be on tour I’d make arrangements to do some teaching as well. I get a lot of enjoyment out of that and there’s a lot of energy. And I started the organization in the States in Cedar Rapids, Iowa. I didn’t start it in New York. I started it there, it’s not far from the University of Iowa, but my kids were there. My two sons were there so I was making visits there so I said well let me set it up here. I was connected with a number of musicians and people in the community because when I’d go there I’d play, and we got registered there and being a small market there was only so much could be done, so I keep the registration there, we moved to New York, I set up here in New York so, and it’s grown. It’s grown immensely.

They both played when they were very young but my oldest son, he’s a football and track coach at the high school he graduated from. And his brother, who is a year and a half younger, he works for a Hospice organization.
